Sentiment is bad – a good thing. That's when value is found. It's not generally found outside of that setting.

So, "the price is concerning me" is simply an emotionally-influenced decision vs a logical one. One should be thrilled to buy a fundamentally solid stock down 71% off of its highs.

It's been around since 1951. 800.000 employees. $78 billion company. Forward P/E in the 8's. Almost $13 billion earned in a "bad year" for them, last year. Over $10 billion in cash. What's scary about that? These are the situations we long for...not the ones we shrink back from.

Yep, tons of institutions hold it, correct (and they're in at MUCH higher prices than we are). And yes, only 4.7% of shares are short. So, there's not a lot of conviction to short and huge conviction to own, by the big boys/institutions.

It's why we're never moved/motivated by news/analysts, etc. We're moved by measurable fundamentals.

Warren Buffett talks about how the world is yours if you can keep your head about you when others lose theirs. Well, how do we do that so consistently? We do it through tracking measurable fundamentals (fundamental strength/fundamental cheapness). From that point, it's about measurable technicals/sentiment/wave counts, etc.

Buffett also says that you have to hold your nose and buy (meaning that when there are the best times to be buying, things stink, in the news/sentiment, etc.

The way you're naturally inclined to think/feel about a stock will mislead you. It's why we ONLY use measurable metrics (fundamentals/technicals/sentiment/Elliott Waves). I never ask myself how I feel about a stock. It's irrelevant and if anything would lead us astray and we'd have mixed results from being fickle/reactionary.

You're welcome. And anything that I say that can be perceived as a negative is just really analytical thought and never meant to be harsh/negative. But just to be helpful in aiding someone in pushing through the emotions back to logic.

Emotions (in every area of life) are great followers and horrible leaders. Yet, most people allow them to lead in stock-picking, marriage, business, etc.

It's why Warren Buffett's biggest message is one where a person has to have a total contrarian outlook to the masses: Be greedy when others are fearful and be fearful when others are greedy.

In other words, see opportunity when all others see is fear. When everyone is in love with a stock, learn to shun that, etc., is another way to say what Buffett is saying.

We're getting into Vintagio (VTG) now. Yes, it's a beer/wine company. However, when you buy shares, the company doesn't get the cash...the share holder (or specialist) that sold you the shares gets the cash. So, it doesn't enrich the company or fund/fuel the company.

When you buy an IPO (primary market) or pre-IPO, you fund the company. If you buy into a secondary offering, you fund the company. But when you buy into the secondary/public market and buy shares, you aren't giving money to the company.

So, if you don't buy their beer/wine, etc. then you're not funding them. If you didn't buy their IPO/pre-IPO, then you're not funding them.

YET...even though we're not giving the company money, by owning shares, we'd reap a 3% dividend yield and the beer/wine company would be paying us 3% per year in dividends, while we hold it. (The wealth of the wicked is laid up for the righteous).

VTG is a $23 billion, defensive consumer company. Forward P/E of 11 (cheap).

20% profit margin

Almost $3,5 billion earned, in a bad year for them.

Not quite $100 million in cash (small) but they have the free cash flow to keep up their dividend and fund buybacks.

Just over $10 billion in debt, which is still healthy for a $23 billion company.

So it's fundamentally solid and fundamentally cheap. So, why invest now?
